title: The good I would (Romans 7:15–25)
hook: Paul admits he does what he hates

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptizo: buried with him in baptism. Your line was newness of life. What did you leave in the water? Day five hundred sixty-four.

January first: a resolution on a sticky note. No more scrolling in bed. January third, one in the morning: a phone glowing in the dark, the sticky note still on the mirror. The gap between what a person means to do and what they actually do is an old one. Paul's letters can sound lofty and sure of themselves. Chapter seven of Romans does not. In it, Paul describes that gap in the first person, with no excuses.
screen: `JANUARY FIRST: A RESOLUTION.` → `JANUARY THIRD, 1 A.M.` → `PAUL NAMES THE GAP.`

segments.voice: In Romans 7, Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "For that which I work, I understand not. For I do not that good which I will; but the evil which I hate, that I do." A few lines later he says it again, almost like a man pacing a room: "For the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will not, that I do." Older English put it as the good I would: would in the old sense of what I want, what I will. He agrees the law is good. He wants the good. And something in him pulls the other way. He calls it sin dwelling in me, a different law at war in his members. And then the cry: "Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" That's not a theologian's polished sentence. It's a groan. But it doesn't end there. The very next line answers: "The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord." The Greek reads, thanks be to God. Either way, the answer isn't a better resolution. It's a person. Now, honesty: readers have argued for centuries about who the I in this chapter is. Some, including Saint Augustine in his later writings, read it as Paul describing his life as a believer, still struggling. Others read it as Paul looking back at life before Christ, or speaking for humanity in Adam's shoes. The Church hasn't required one reading. What Catholics do recognize here is something the tradition calls concupiscence: an inclination toward sin that remains even after baptism, not itself sin, but the place where the struggle happens. Paul doesn't hide it. He names the divided heart, and then he points to grace.
screen: `THE GOOD WHICH I WILL, I DO NOT.` · `A LAW AT WAR IN MY MEMBERS.` · `UNHAPPY MAN THAT I AM.` · `WHO IS THE I?` · then, large: `THE GRACE OF GOD, BY JESUS CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your divided heart. Settle, and breathe. Name, silently, one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Not ten things. One. Don't argue with yourself, don't make a plan yet. Just let it be true, the way Paul let it be true on the page. Notice that naming it is already different from hiding it. Then, if you pray, you can borrow Paul's own words: who shall deliver me, and, the grace of God, by Jesus Christ. If you don't, simply breathe out, and let the honesty be enough for today. The bell holds the time.
Wretched. Paul's own word for himself in Romans seven, unhappy man that I am, caught between the good he wills and the evil he does. Today's word.
Your line: who shall deliver me. Today, when you catch yourself in the gap, don't hide it: name it, and ask for help. Day five hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics bring the struggle Paul describes to the sacrament of reconciliation, naming their sins to a priest and receiving absolution, and some make a nightly examination of conscience.

fork.setup: you're writing to a church you've never met, wanting them to trust you. do you admit your own inner struggle?
options: no; present yourself as having it together.
yes; name it plainly, then point to who delivers.
fork.reveal: Paul writes it in the first person: the evil which I hate, that I do. then he names the answer: the grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord.

original.note: Greek: wretched, miserable, worn down. unhappy man that I am, in the Douay-Rheims.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was a saint who had it all together.
what it means: he admits in writing that he does what he hates, cries out for deliverance, and points to God's grace in the next breath.

what a scholar hears: who the I is has been argued since the early Church. Augustine changed his own mind, coming to read it as a believer's struggle; other readers, ancient and modern, read it differently.

notes: Augustine's change of view (earlier: pre-conversion humanity; later, e.g. Retractations and anti-Pelagian works: the believer): confirm.
Concupiscence remains after baptism and is not itself sin (Trent, Session V; CCC 1264, 2515): confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): All four Romans 7 quotations were KJV; now Douay-Rheims. The Douay of 7:25 reads 'The grace of God, by Jesus Christ our Lord' (following the Vulgate), not 'I thank God'; the script now says so and gives the Greek sense ('thanks be to God'), and screens, games and practice follow. Hook no longer tells the listener what they did or claims 'almost everyone'; cut 'one of the most important writers'. Douay wording checked against drbo.org.
